alm_analemma_desc: The figure-8 the Sun traces over a year, photographed at the same clock time each day.
alm_dt_daylen_desc: The Moon’s gravity creates tides that act like brakes on Earth’s spin. Each century, days grow 1.8ms longer. Since the year 2000, days have stretched {ms}ms. Doesn’t sound like much, but 600 million years ago, a day was only 21 hours. The Moon drifts 3.8 cm farther each year, slowly releasing its grip.
alm_dt_galactic_desc: The Sun orbits the Milky Way’s center every ~225 million years at 828,000 km/h. In {age} billion years, we’ve completed roughly {orbits} orbits. Last time we were here, dinosaurs ruled the Earth.
alm_dt_julian_desc: A continuous count of days since January 1, 4713 BC. Used by astronomers because it never resets, skips, or changes with calendar reforms. Every event in human history has exactly one Julian Date. Immune to leap seconds, timezone changes, and political calendars.
alm_dt_orbit_desc: How elliptical Earth’s orbit is (0 = perfect circle, 1 = extremely stretched). Currently near-circular and {trend}. This affects how much solar energy Earth receives over a year. Combined with tilt and precession, these three cycles drive ice ages (Milanković theory).
alm_dt_polaris_desc: Earth wobbles like a spinning top. Polaris happens to be near the axis right now, but it’s drifting. Closest alignment ~2100 (0.45°), then it drifts away. In ~{years} years, Vega will be the “North Star.” Full wobble cycle: 25,772 years.
alm_dt_tilt_desc: This tilt is why seasons exist. It’s currently {trend}, meaning: {impact}. Cycles between 22.1° and 24.5° over 41,000 years (Milanković cycle). Currently {pct}% through the cycle.
alm_footer: All calculations are math-driven and work offline forever.

alm_orr_twin_explain: While the ship coasts, each twin sees the other’s clock run slow, so it looks like a tie. It is not: only the traveller feels the engines, and while the speed changes, the traveller’s idea of what time it is on Earth right now jumps ahead. Add those jumps up and the traveller ends up {lag} younger.

ref_decay_link: What stops being true without updates
ref_far_year: This year is far from the present: the Earth's spin is not known exactly then, so clock times may be off by minutes or more. Positions among the stars still hold.
ref_daily_lede: Greenwich hour angle (GHA) and declination for each hour of Universal Time, as the Nautical Almanac tabulates them.
ref_daily_how: For a time between the hours, add to the hour's GHA: 15° per hour (15′ a minute) for the Sun and planets, 15°02.5′ per hour for Aries, 14°19′ per hour for the Moon plus v times the fraction of the hour. Declination changes by d per hour. A star's GHA is GHA Aries plus its SHA. SD is semi-diameter and HP horizontal parallax, both in minutes of arc.
ref_daily_accuracy: Checked against the U.S. Naval Observatory's almanac data: Sun and stars within 0.2′, Moon and planets within 0.5′.
ref_low_altitude: Below 5° refraction is unreliable: a sight this low can be off by several miles.
ref_below_horizon: At that time and place the body was below the horizon. Check the time, the date and the body.
ref_lop_answer: Your line of position runs {a}°–{b}° through {pos}.
ref_plot_label: Plotting sheet: the assumed position, the azimuth and the line of position
ref_noon_sight_text: If this was the body at its highest, your latitude is {lat} (it bore {bearing}). At this longitude the Sun is highest at {time} UT that day.
ref_sight_how: Take several sights of the same body and average them. Mark the assumed position, draw the azimuth Zn through it, step off the intercept toward the body (or away), and draw the line of position square to the azimuth. Two or three bodies at different bearings cross at your fix.
ref_eclipse_seen_solar: Seen here: {kind}, {pct}% of the Sun's width covered at {time}, from {from} to {to}.
ref_eclipse_seen_lunar: Seen here: {kind}, umbral magnitude {mag} at {time}, the Moon in shadow from {from} to {to}.
ref_year_notes: Times are local clock times, daylight saving included. Sunrise and sunset are the Sun's upper edge on a flat horizon; dawn and dusk are the Sun 18° (astronomical), 12° (nautical) and 6° (civil) below it. Height is the Sun's at noon. A dash: it does not happen that day.
ref_suntime_lede: A sundial shows the Sun's own time. Your clock keeps an even time for a whole time zone. The difference changes through the year; this page gives it for every day.
ref_analemma_caption: Across: the equation of time, minutes the Sun runs fast (right) or slow. Up: its declination. A dot on the first of each month.
ref_correction_how: Read the sundial, then add the day's figure to get the time on your clock (daylight saving included). The figure folds together the equation of time and how far your place lies from your time zone's meridian.
ref_stars_lede: Before calendars were written down, years were counted by the first morning a bright star could be seen again before sunrise: Sirius for the Nile's flood, the Pleiades for planting and Matariki.
ref_star_never: Never high enough to see from here: {names}.
ref_star_always: Never set here, so never lost to the Sun: {names}.
ref_star_seen: Seen in some part of the night all year: {names}.
ref_stars_how: Look low in the east in the last of the dawn twilight. A clear, flat horizon is assumed; haze or hills move these dates a few days, so read each as about. The rule: the Sun about 10° below the horizon, less for a brighter star.
ref_cal_lede: Pick a date in any calendar to see it in all the others. The Islamic dates are the tabular (arithmetic) calendar; where the month begins with the sighted crescent, it can fall a day or two later.
ref_feasts_notes: Jewish festivals begin at sunset the evening before. * From the tabular Islamic calendar; local sighting may differ by a day or two. Nowruz is the day the March equinox falls before noon in Tehran; Chinese New Year is the second new moon after the winter solstice, in China's time.
ref_decay_lede: Most of what the Almanac shows is arithmetic that will hold for centuries. A few things come from outside and slowly go stale without updates. Here is each one, how old this machine's copy is, and what goes wrong as it ages.
ref_deltat_age: model {model} s now; measured {measured} s in {year}
ref_d_tz_text: Governments change their clocks a few times a year somewhere. Clock times here use this device's own copy of the rules; after a change it has not heard of, local times for that place are an hour off. Universal Time and Sun time are unaffected.
ref_d_sats_text: The Earth view places the GPS satellites and the ISS from their published orbits. They drift a few kilometres a day; after weeks the ISS's place is a guess, after months only its orbit's shape is right.
ref_d_deltat_text: The Earth's rotation slows unevenly and can only be measured, not predicted. A model fills the gap; each second it is off moves the Moon by half a second of arc, and an eclipse track by half a kilometre. Over a century the error can grow to minutes.
ref_d_leap_text: Clocks keep UTC, which has had leap seconds inserted to follow the Earth. None has been added since 2016 and they are due to stop by 2035. Navigation needs UT1, within 0.9 s of UTC: at most 0.2′ of longitude.
ref_d_catalog_text: The list of downloadable books and wikis is a copy from the last time this machine was online. New titles and newer editions will not appear in it.
ref_h_calendars_text: The Gregorian, Julian, Hebrew and tabular Islamic calendars, and Easter, are pure arithmetic: right for any year.
ref_h_sky_text: Their positions come from published theories (VSOP87, Meeus) good for centuries; only clock times inherit the uncertainty of the Earth's spin.
ref_h_stars_text: Their places include their own motions and the slow wobble of the Earth's axis, so star tables stay right for centuries.
ref_h_seasons_text: Equinoxes, solstices and the Moon's phases follow from the same arithmetic, to a minute or two over the next few centuries.
ref_noon_sight_when: At this longitude the Sun is highest at {time} UT that day. Measure it then, at its highest, and this page gives your latitude directly.

tb_sunmoon_note: Local clock times, daylight saving included. Sunrise and sunset are the Sun’s upper edge on a flat horizon; noon height is the Sun’s altitude as it crosses the meridian. A dash: it does not happen that day.
tb_twilight_note: Dawn and dusk are the Sun 18° (astronomical), 12° (nautical) and 6° (civil) below the horizon. Civil twilight is light enough to read by; nautical, to see the sea’s horizon; astronomical, the last of the sky’s glow.
tb_tide_none: Tides are worked out for the Almanac’s place when it is near a coast. Choose a place on the Almanac’s map.
tb_tide_far: Tide predictions are offered within {n} years of today.
tb_no_star: No bright star returns or leaves in this window.
tb_seasons_note: Local clock times. Each season runs from its instant to the next; the Earth moves fastest in January, so the northern winter is the shortest.
tb_no_eclipse: No eclipse falls in this window.
tb_sundial_how: Read the sundial and add the correction to get the time on your clock. The equation of time is how far the Sun runs ahead of an even clock; the longitude part is how far your place lies from the meridian your clock keeps (daylight saving moves that meridian an hour east).
tb_days_note: Julian Day Number {a} less {b} is {n}: days counted straight through, without months or years, the way astronomers count them.
tb_zones_note: Each place’s zone is that of the nearest of the Almanac’s time-zone cities; offsets include daylight saving on that date, by the rules this device knows.
tb_bearing_sub: Set off on a bearing of {a}°, arrive heading {b}°
tb_gc_note: The shortest path on a sphere (the haversine formula). The Earth’s flattening changes a long distance by up to half a percent. A ship or a plane on this great circle crosses each meridian at a different bearing.
tb_units_note: Exact by definition: the inch is 25.4 mm, the pound 0.45359237 kg, the US gallon 231 cubic inches, the imperial gallon 4.54609 L, the knot one nautical mile (1,852 m) an hour, the standard atmosphere 101,325 Pa.
tb_sundial_clock: When the sundial reads noon, your clock reads {time}.
tb_hint_body: What you measured: the Sun, the Moon, a planet or a star.
tb_hint_limb: Which edge of the disc you brought down to the horizon; usually the lower.
tb_hint_when: The moment of the sight in Universal Time, to the second if you can.
tb_hint_hs: What the sextant read, before any correction.
tb_hint_ie: What the sextant reads with the horizon lined up in both mirrors. Above zero (on the arc) is taken off; below zero is added.
tb_hint_eye: How far your eye was above the water. The higher you stand, the further the horizon dips.
tb_hint_temp: For refraction: cold air bends light more. 10 °C is standard.
tb_hint_pressure: For refraction too: dense air bends light more. 1,010 hPa is standard.
tb_hint_lat: Where you think you are (your dead reckoning). The answer moves you from here.
tb_hint_lon: The same estimate, east or west.
tb_mm_sun: Sun: VSOP87D, with nutation and aberration (Meeus ch. 22, 23, 25)
tb_mm_rise: Sunrise and sunset: the Sun's centre at {alt}, refraction {r} plus semidiameter {sd}
tb_mm_moonrise: Moonrise and moonset: {k} × horizontal parallax minus refraction {r} (Meeus ch. 15)
tb_mm_twilight: Twilight: the Sun {c}°, {n}° and {a}° below the horizon
tb_mm_search: Events: positions every {h} h, crossings checked every {m} min, bisected to about {s} s
tb_mm_phases: Phases: the Moon's longitude minus the Sun's at {list}
tb_mm_eclipses: Eclipses: what this place sees, every {m} min for {h} h either side of greatest
tb_mm_planets: Planets: VSOP87, light time and aberration (Meeus ch. 33)
tb_mm_stars: Stars: catalogue places with proper motion, precession (Meeus ch. 21), aberration and nutation
tb_mm_heliacal: First and last sightings: the Sun {av}° plus the star's magnitude below the horizon as the star stands at {alt}
tb_mm_sight: Sight reduction: dip {k}′ × √(eye height in m); refraction at {t} °C and {p} hPa
tb_mm_tides: Tides: NOAA harmonic constants for {station}, {n} constituents
tb_mm_tides_world: Tides: TICON-3 harmonic constants for {station}, {n} constituents
tb_mm_tides_sub: Tides: highs and lows from {ref} with NOAA's offsets for {station}; a half cosine between them
tb_mm_eot: Equation of time: apparent minus mean solar time
tb_mm_calendars: Calendars: {list}, each by its own rules
tb_mm_distance: Distance: great circle (haversine) on a sphere of radius {r} km
tb_mm_zones: Times: the browser's time zone database (IANA)

alm_blurb_sun: A star so big that it holds nearly all the Solar System's mass.
alm_blurb_earth: The only world known to have life, and oceans of liquid water.
alm_blurb_moon: Always shows Earth the same face, and its pull raises the tides.
alm_blurb_iss: A home in orbit where people have lived without a break since 2000.
alm_blurb_mercury: The smallest planet, scorching by day and freezing by night.
alm_blurb_venus: The hottest planet, wrapped in thick clouds and spinning backwards.
alm_blurb_mars: A cold red desert with the tallest volcano in the Solar System.
alm_blurb_jupiter: The biggest planet, with a storm that has raged for centuries.
alm_blurb_saturn: Famous for its icy rings, and lighter than water for its size.
alm_blurb_uranus: An ice giant that spins on its side, rolling around the Sun.
alm_blurb_neptune: An ice giant, blue from methane, with the fastest winds in the Solar System.
alm_blurb_pluto: A dwarf planet with a giant heart-shaped plain of frozen nitrogen.
alm_blurb_ceres: The largest world in the asteroid belt, with bright salty spots.
alm_blurb_io: The most volcanic world known, with eruptions that never stop.
alm_blurb_europa: Under its icy shell hides a salty ocean, maybe with more water than Earth.
alm_blurb_ganymede: The biggest moon in the Solar System, larger than the planet Mercury.
alm_blurb_callisto: An ancient moon, one of the most crater-covered places in the Solar System.
alm_blurb_titan: The only moon with thick air, and lakes of liquid methane.
alm_blurb_voyager1: The first spacecraft to leave the Sun's bubble, carrying a golden record.
alm_blurb_voyager2: The only spacecraft to visit Uranus and Neptune, in interstellar space since 2018.
alm_blurb_pioneer10: The first to cross the asteroid belt and fly past Jupiter, carrying a plaque for aliens.
alm_blurb_pioneer11: The first to see Saturn up close, carrying a plaque for anyone who finds it.
alm_blurb_newhorizons: Gave us the first close look at Pluto, then flew on to a snowman-shaped rock.
alm_blurb_parker: Flies closer to the Sun than anything we have built, through its outer atmosphere.
alm_blurb_juno: Circles Jupiter from pole to pole, peering beneath its clouds.
alm_blurb_jwst: A gold-mirrored telescope that sees the oldest galaxies in infrared light.
alm_blurb_cassini: Spent years at Saturn and sent a lander down to Titan.
alm_blurb_galileo: The first spacecraft to orbit Jupiter, and it dropped a probe into its clouds.
alm_blurb_europaclipper: On its way to Jupiter to study Europa's hidden ocean.
alm_blurb_solarorbiter: Looks at the Sun's poles, which no spacecraft had seen before.
alm_blurb_psyche: Heading for Psyche, a lump of metal that may be the core of a lost world.
alm_blurb_lucy: Visits the Trojan asteroids, leftovers from the birth of the planets.
alm_blurb_hubble: A space telescope above the atmosphere, seeing the universe sharply since 1990.
alm_blurb_chandra: An X-ray telescope that sees hot gas, black holes and exploding stars.
alm_blurb_juice: Going to Jupiter's icy moons, and will orbit Ganymede.
alm_blurb_osirisapex: Delivered rock from the asteroid Bennu, and now flies to Apophis.
alm_blurb_hayabusa2: Returned dust from the asteroid Ryugu and flew on to a new one.

tb_scene_note: The sky is computed, not photographed: its air follows Hillaire's 2020 atmosphere model with the Earth's published scattering coefficients, and the same tables draw the card, Look and Stand here. The clouds are not weather (Zimi has none): one deck of cloud is generated for each place and day, the same all day and new the next. Its cover is chosen evenly from thin to heavy, and its height, thickness and wind are the figures above. A visit to see something in the sky (an eclipse, a there and then) opens with a clear sky.

tb_kn_pv_view: Stand at the pad: where you stand
tb_kn_pv_view_v: 2.5 km from LC-39A on bearing 200° and 4 km from SLC-41 on 215°, eye 1.7 m over the ground, facing the pad. The distances are assumed (a press site's for that class of vehicle), not surveyed spots. The count starts at T−30 s on the mission's own clock.
tb_kn_pv_climb: Stand at the pad: the first seconds of the climb
tb_kn_pv_climb_v: The mission's table has a row every 10 to 20 s, too coarse for lift-off. From lift-off to the first row 15 s later (T+25 s for Apollo 11, T+22 s for Mars 2020) the climb is fitted to that row: straight up with a constant jerk, and the downrange drift a power of the time that meets the table's. The vehicle stands still until lift-off (T+0.6 s for Apollo 11) and clears the tower when its foot passes 122 m (about T+10 s).
tb_kn_pv_pad: Stand at the pad: the launch structures
tb_kn_pv_pad_v: LC-39A is the site model of the mobile launcher and umbilical tower (122 m, lightning mast to 134 m); its swing arms do not move. SLC-41 is boxes: a 48 × 40 × 9 m apron, a platform deck, a 56 m umbilical tower and four 100 m lightning masts. The proportions are approximate, not a replica.
tb_kn_pv_exhaust: Stand at the pad: flame, cloud and trail
tb_kn_pv_exhaust_v: The flame lengths are the mission's own (60 m for the Saturn V's first stage, longer as the air thins). The cloud at the pad, the sparks and the trail are puffs of assumed size, speed and life, not a fluid simulation: a trail puff every 12 m of the way, up to 30 km high. No weather is drawn: the sky is the clear one.
alm_gr_omitted: In this edition, the pictures that are not public domain are named, not shown.
alm_gr_note: Eight of these pictures are NASA photographs, in the public domain. The rest are copyright their owners, named beside each picture: Jon Lomberg, UN Photo, Frank Drake, the National Astronomy and Ionosphere Center, Jay M. Pasachoff and Picturepoint, London. They appear here so the record can be seen as it was sent; Zimi claims no rights in them. These are NASA's scans of the original pictures, not decoded from the record's sound.
